expect:
Top band (10-12): Injection moulding: molten polymer is forced under high pressure into a precision steel mould cavity; the polymer cools and the mould opens to eject the part; produces complex, high-detail parts with tight tolerances; very fast cycle time; high tooling cost offset by large volumes; ideal for solid, small, complex parts like bottle caps — the thread, tamper-evident band and sealing ring need dimensional precision. Blow moulding: a hot polymer parison (tube) is clamped in a split mould and compressed air inflates it to fill the mould cavity; used for hollow thin-walled containers; produces lightweight, seamless, hollow forms; PET bottles need thin walls and uniform thickness — achievable by blow moulding, not by injection moulding (which would require enormous material volume for a hollow bottle). Discussion of why each process suits its product and not the other's: injection moulding cannot produce a thin-walled hollow bottle efficiently; blow moulding cannot achieve the fine surface detail and thread precision of a bottle cap. Accurate spelling, punctuation and grammar throughout.
Upper-mid band (7-9): Both processes described well with reasonable comparison.
Lower-mid band (4-6): One process described in detail, other briefly.
Lower band (1-3): Superficial or confused description of processes.
value:
Top band (8-10): Injection moulding: molten polymer is forced under high pressure into a precision steel mould cavity; the polymer cools and the mould opens to eject the part; produces complex, high-detail parts with tight tolerances; very fast cycle time; high tooling cost offset by large volumes; ideal for solid, small, complex parts like bottle caps — the thread, tamper-evident band and sealing ring need dimensional precision. Blow moulding: a hot polymer tube or preform is clamped in a split mould and compressed air inflates it to fill the mould cavity; PET bottles use injection stretch blow moulding, in which an injection-moulded preform is reheated, stretched with a rod and then blown; used for hollow thin-walled containers; produces lightweight, seamless, hollow forms; PET bottles need thin walls and uniform thickness — achievable by blow moulding, not by injection moulding (which would require enormous material volume for a hollow bottle). Discussion of why each process suits its product and not the other's: injection moulding cannot produce a thin-walled hollow bottle efficiently; blow moulding cannot achieve the fine surface detail and thread precision of a bottle cap.
Upper-mid band (6-7): Both processes described well with reasonable comparison.
Lower-mid band (4-5): One process described in detail, other briefly.
Low band (1-3): Superficial or confused description of processes.
